title: The accidental bell
teaches: FM: a vibrato so fast it becomes new harmonics, and why bells clang

blocks.text: **The sound.** A bell is one of the hardest sounds to make with a filter. Start from a bright saw, take harmonics away, and whatever you do it sounds like a note, never a clang. Yet here is a bell from the synth, made from nothing but two sine waves.

blocks.caption: A sine wave struck like a bell, and the same sine with a second one hidden inside it

blocks.text: It was found by accident. In 1967 [[John Chowning]], a young composer at Stanford, was playing with vibrato on a computer. He had a programme that could swing the pitch of one tone with another, as an LFO does, and he did what anyone does with a new control: he turned it up. Faster than a singer, faster than a spinning organ speaker, into the hundreds of wobbles a second. At that speed the wobble vanished. Instead the tone changed colour. It became brassy, or hollow, or rang like a bell, and a tiny change in the numbers moved it from one to the other.[^chowning]

blocks.caption: John Chowning, who found FM synthesis at Stanford in 1967.

blocks.text: He had found **[[FM synthesis]]**: frequency modulation at audio rates. One oscillator, the **modulator**, swings the pitch of another, the **carrier**, so fast that the ear hears new harmonics instead of a wobble. It took two oscillators to make sounds that subtractive synthesis needed dozens of parts to fake, and nobody had noticed because nobody had thought to turn vibrato up that far.

blocks.caption: A sine wave, with a hidden oscillator swinging its pitch. Amount is how far it swings.

parts.title: Where the new harmonics come from

blocks.text: Swing a pitch around fast and its spectrum grows **sidebands**: new lines on either side of the carrier, spaced by the modulator's frequency. A carrier on 220 Hz modulated at 220 Hz grows lines at 440, 660, 880: the harmonics of the note. The further the pitch swings (the **index**), the more lines appear, and their sizes rise and fall in a pattern that mathematicians had worked out a century and a half earlier for the motion of planets, the Bessel functions.[^bessel]

blocks.caption: The spectrum of FM: a carrier on 220 Hz, and the lines that grow either side of it. Pick the modulator's ratio to the carrier and turn up the index.
blocks.task: Find a clang: a ratio that is not a whole number, with the index at 2 or more

blocks.text: FM radio uses the same mathematics, with a carrier at a hundred million cycles a second and your voice as the modulator.[^radio] The sidebands are why stations must be spaced apart on the dial.

On the synth, **Ratio** is how fast the modulator runs compared with the note. ×1 fills in every harmonic, like brass. ×2 gives only the odd ones, hollow like a square. ×3 and ×4 leave gaps in the stack, with some harmonics missing and strong lines far above the note, which already sounds metallic. ×½ adds a line an octave below, a growl.

blocks.caption: The FM ratio, with the amount part way up.

blocks.text: A struck bell does not make a stack of harmonics. Its metal shell flexes in several shapes at once, and their frequencies are not whole-number multiples of one note: a well-tuned church bell has a hum tone an octave below the note, a prime on the note, a minor third (which gives bells their faintly sad sound), a fifth and more, and the higher ones drift off any harmonic series.[^bellmodes] Our ears try to fit them to one note and can't, and that failure is the clang. FM with a ratio that puts sidebands between the harmonics does the same, which is why it makes such convincing bells, chimes and electric pianos. This synth's Ratio knob has only whole numbers (above ×½), so its bells are a near miss: ×3 or ×4 with plenty of amount piles strong, widely spaced lines high above the note, and on a struck envelope the ear hears metal. The sidebands figure above goes further, to a ratio such as ×3.5, where the lines fall between the harmonics and the clang is real.

blocks.caption: Two knobs as one square: across is the ratio, up is the amount.
blocks.task: Find a bell: ratio ×3 or ×4, amount 2 or more

blocks.text: Stanford patented Chowning's discovery and licensed it to Yamaha in 1973. In 1983 Yamaha put it in the **[[DX7]]**, a keyboard with six sine oscillators per voice and no filter at all. It cost a fraction of the big polyphonic analogue synths and sounded like nothing else: glassy electric pianos, punchy basses, bells. It became one of the best-selling synthesizers ever made, and for a few years its preset electric piano was on what feels like every pop ballad.[^royalties]

blocks.caption: A Yamaha DX7. Its sounds were edited one number at a time with buttons and a single slider, and many owners never went past the factory sounds.

events.label: Chowning turns vibrato up into the audio range
Stanford licenses the patent to Yamaha

blocks.text: FM on a sine is the clean case. On a brighter wave every harmonic grows sidebands of its own, and the sound becomes rough quickly.

blocks.caption: The wave selector and the FM amount.
blocks.task: On the saw, raise Amount until you can clearly hear it

blocks.text: Back to the bell from the start. Its envelope is already set: struck, no sustain, a long ring. What remains is the FM. On this synth the nearest thing to a clang is a ratio with gaps, and the amount sets how bright the strike is.

blocks.caption: Two sines, struck like a bell, with the FM off: bring it in.

blocks.text: A real bell's overtones start bright and the high ones die first. The DX7 sends each note's envelope to the FM amount as well, so the strike rings with metal then mellows into a hum: two sines and an envelope, a better bell than a room of filters.

blocks.caption: Six questions on FM
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What did Chowning do to discover FM synthesis?
choices: Turned a vibrato's rate up into the hundreds of cycles a second
Built a new kind of filter
Recorded a bell and slowed it down
items.why: An audio-rate vibrato is no longer heard as a wobble but as new harmonics.

items.ask: A carrier on 300 Hz is modulated at 100 Hz. Where do the first sidebands appear?
items.why: Sidebands sit either side of the carrier, spaced by the modulator's frequency.

items.ask: What does turning up the FM index (the amount) do?
choices: Adds more sidebands, so a brighter sound
items.why: The further the pitch swings, the more sidebands carry energy.

items.ask: Why does FM with a ratio like ×3.5 sound like a bell?
choices: Its sidebands fall between the harmonics, as a bell's tones do
items.why: Bells have overtones that aren't whole-number multiples of one note; the ear hears that as a clang.

items.ask: What did the DX7 lack that most earlier synths had?
items.why: It built its sounds by FM alone, with six sine oscillators per voice.

items.ask: What do FM radio and FM synthesis share?
items.why: Both swing one frequency with another; only the speeds differ.

summary: **FM is a vibrato so fast it becomes timbre**, found by Chowning at Stanford in 1967.
**Swinging a carrier's pitch grows sidebands**, spaced by the modulator's frequency; more swing, more sidebands.
**Whole-number ratios keep the sidebands on harmonics**: a note, brassy or hollow, or metallic when the ratio leaves gaps.
**Other ratios put them between harmonics**: a clang, like a bell, whose tones aren't a harmonic series.
**The DX7 (1983) made FM the sound of the 1980s**: six sine oscillators per voice and no filter.
**FM radio is the same mathematics** at a hundred million cycles a second.

chowning.title: Chowning's computer
chowning.text: Chowning worked on the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory's computer with Max Mathews's MUSIC programmes, which computed sound sample by sample and could take minutes to render seconds of music. Nothing about FM needed special hardware; it was simply a setting nobody had tried.

bessel.title: Bessel functions
bessel.text: Friedrich Bessel studied them in 1817 for the motion of a planet in an elliptical orbit (Daniel Bernoulli had met the first ones earlier in hanging chains). The size of the k-th sideband is the Bessel function Jₖ of the index. At an index of about 2.4 the carrier itself vanishes entirely, leaving only sidebands: a trick radio engineers use to calibrate transmitters.

radio.title: Armstrong's static-free radio
radio.text: Edwin Armstrong patented FM broadcasting in 1933 to beat the crackle of AM radio, since lightning and motors change a signal's strength but hardly its frequency. RCA, which had bet on AM, fought him for decades. FM stations broadcast between 88 and 108 million cycles a second.

bellmodes.title: The tones of a bell
bellmodes.text: Bell founders tune five main overtones (or partials) in a church bell. Above the hum note come the prime, a minor third (the tierce), a fifth (the quint) and the nominal an octave above the prime; the higher partials no founder can tune fall where the shape puts them. The note we hear as the bell's pitch, the strike note, isn't any one of these: the ear invents it from the pattern.

royalties.title: Stanford's royalties
royalties.text: The FM patent earned Stanford more than twenty million dollars before it expired in 1995, at the time the university's second most lucrative licence. Yamaha sold about 200,000 DX7s.
